summary:
Karachay-Cherkessia stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have risen eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night, The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

That same note singles out the North Caucasus, including Karachay-Cherkessia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in these republics are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note records systematic regional campaigns between 2017 and 2024, and states that the 2023 extremist designation carries two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising activity.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, reports that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He describes year-on-year deterioration across the North Caucasus republics he covers as an on-the-ground defender in exile, Karachay-Cherkessia among them.
tangentialFactors:
The North Caucasus finding cuts against the general tenor of the UK Home Office assessment, which otherwise does not treat Russia as a country of persecution for LGBT+ people. A visitor to Karachay-Cherkessia therefore faces a materially harsher operating environment than the national baseline, and the divergence is documented rather than inferred.

Chechnya is the best-known case of regional persecution inside Russia, but the UK note extends the same treatment-amounting-to-persecution finding to the North Caucasus republics as a group, and the interview evidence covers the region rather than a single republic. Regional patterns of forced return to families and detention reported by David Isteev echo the coercion documented elsewhere in Russia, including the nine-month forced-conversion case near Novosibirsk reported by BBC Russian.

Deterioration is described as continuous rather than episodic: Isteev reports year-on-year worsening, and the UK note's campaign period runs from 2017 to 2024 without a documented end point. Enforcement nationally has also intensified, with propaganda-law cases up eighteenfold over a decade and 101 extremism-related convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch as of 30 June 2025.
localsOnly:

The UK Home Office note records that the extremist designation carries two to six years' imprisonment, and six to ten years where the conduct involves organising. Systematic campaigns across the North Caucasus between 2017 and 2024 form the evidentiary basis for the note's finding that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in these republics are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

For residents, exposure is not limited to public advocacy. Isteev reports that private existence can itself trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that the situation has worsened year on year across the North Caucasus republics.

Under the refugee convention as applied by the UK, LGBT+ people in Russia, including Chechnya, constitute a particular social group, which sets the standard for UK asylum claims and is the basis on which the North Caucasus exception is assessed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No republic-specific court decisions, arrest figures or enforcement statistics for Karachay-Cherkessia itself are sourced here; the regional findings rest on a UK asylum policy note covering the North Caucasus as a group and on one defender's account covering several republics.

The systematic campaigns recorded between 2017 and 2024 are not itemised by republic in the available sources, so the share attributable to Karachay-Cherkessia is unresolved.

Local access to legal gender recognition, gender-affirming care, documentation services and competent medical providers within the republic is not sourced and remains unresolved. The national bans are documented; their practical administration at republic level is not.

No sourced reporting on physical attacks, killings or police conduct specific to Karachay-Cherkessia was available in this inventory, so the level of violence a trans visitor would personally encounter there is unresolved rather than established.
